title: What a stability declaration does to a request, in each caching model
pins: For one hinted conversation: WHICH message carries the cache breakpoint under the mark-in-place model, WHETHER the ordering warning fires under the automatic-prefix model, and WHERE the prefix is split under the create-and-reference model. Those three answers are the whole observable behaviour of a stability hint — everything else about the request is unchanged by it, which is itself pinned by the rows whose answers are all null.
scope: The DERIVATION from a declaration: breakpoint index, ordering warning, prefix split. It does NOT cover whether a provider then actually caches, what a cached resource costs, or the wire format of the cache fields themselves — those belong to each provider's own suite. A green run means three languages derive the same thing from the same declaration, not that caching works.
findings: Recorded at particle-academy/prism v0.129.0, where all three caching models act on the hint in PHP. The TypeScript and Python ports have neither the enum nor the derivation (G-64), so two of three columns are empty and this suite is RED by construction — the failing corpus the ports are built against rather than a description written after them. One row is worth reading before the rest: hint-0005 declares the volatile part FIRST, and the correct answer is no breakpoint, no cached prefix, and a warning. A port that marked something there would look like it was doing more work rather than less, and a corpus that omitted the row would never say so.

discrimination.note: hint-0001 declares nothing and must produce nothing anywhere — the control that fails if a language derives a breakpoint from an undeclared conversation. hint-0004 has an explicit breakpoint already placed, where the correct answer is to leave it alone.

ts.note: G-64: prism-ts has no CacheStability enum and no derivation.

py.note: G-64: prism-py has no CacheStability enum and no derivation.
